subject.title: Not Waving but Drowning
subject.author: Stevie Smith
subject.text:
Nobody heard him, the dead man,   
But still he lay moaning:
I was much further out than you thought   
And not waving but drowning.

Poor chap, he always loved larking larking Playing tricks, kidding, fooling around.
And now he's dead
It must have been too cold for him his heart gave way,   
They said.

Oh, no no no, it was too cold always   
(Still the dead one lay moaning)   
I was much too far out all my life   
And not waving but drowning.

title: Everyone Who Read Her as Waving
standfirst: In April 1953 Stevie Smith told a friend she had written something touching about drowning. Punch thought it was funny. Three months later, at her office desk, so did the people closest to her — and fourteen years after that, so did the committee deciding who should be Poet Laureate.

sections.heading: Three Months Between the Letter and the Desk
sections.body:
On a weekend in April 1953, Stevie Smith wrote to her friend Kay Dick that she had felt "too low for words (eh??) last weekend but worked it off for all that in a poem." She named it in the same letter and guessed, correctly, how it would land: "Punch like it, think it funny I suppose, It was touching, I thought." The critic Matthew Bevis has pointed out that this dating matters more than it looks, since the standard modern edition of Smith's poems places the poem a year later, in 1954 — a discrepancy of no consequence to a reader, but a real one to a biographer, given what happened three months after that April letter.

In July 1953, at her desk at the Newnes publishing house in London, Smith had a breakdown that turned into an attack on her employer, Sir Neville Pearson, with a pair of scissors, and then into a suicide attempt. It ended a career she had held for thirty years. She had been living, since she was three years old, in the same house in Palmers Green, north London, where her aunt raised her after her father left the family for a life at sea. The poem she had written in April had already described, almost to the word, what the people around her would fail to notice in July: someone signalling from much further out than anyone thought.

sections.heading: The Comma She Cut
sections.body:
The poem is built as three six-line stanzas rhyming only on their second and fourth lines — moaning and drowning, dead and said, moaning and drowning again — a pattern scholars call a nonce form: invented for this poem, never reused. Inside that loose, rocking structure Smith does something more exact. An earlier version of the closing phrase carried a comma: not waving, but drowning. She removed it. Bevis argues the cut comma "makes the words more piercing in their very refusal to pause" — with the comma gone, the drowning arrives with no breath between it and the waving everyone mistook it for.

The same withholding runs through the poem's most awkward line: "It must have been too cold for him his heart gave way, / They said" — six short, mostly single-syllable words running on without a joining word, as flat and toneless as the bystanders delivering it. And the poem's own word for the body shifts, almost imperceptibly, between its first and third stanzas: "the dead man" becomes "the dead one." Even Smith's own accompanying drawing refuses to resolve anything. It shows not a man but a girl, waist-deep in water with wet hair over her face, wearing what one scholar has called a mysterious smile — a second ambiguous signal laid directly on top of the first.

sections.heading: Punch Read It Exactly the Way She Said It Would
sections.body:
Smith's prediction in that April letter came true. Punch published the poem, and — by her own account in the same letter — its editors took it as comedy rather than the touching thing she had meant. It was not the first time this happened to her. When her first collection, A Good Time Was Had by All, appeared in 1937, drawn from what she called about ten years of illicit office scribbling, the Times Literary Supplement filed its review under the heading "humour." Nursery-rhyme metre, plain words, a chatty, undercutting tone: the same qualities that let Smith smuggle death and abandonment into poems short enough to read in thirty seconds were the qualities that got the poems read as jokes.

What survived that misreading is the more interesting fact. Neither the joke publication nor the humour classification stopped "Not Waving but Drowning" becoming, within Smith's own lifetime, the poem she was most identified with. But it also meant that the very mechanism the poem describes — a distress signal read as a wave because the reader would rather it were one — was something Smith kept living through rather than only writing about.

sections.heading: A Star Turn at the Festival Hall
sections.body:
By the 1960s, poetry readings had turned a fifty-something former secretary into something closer to a stage act. Smith performed her poems rather than simply reading them, chanting two or three at a time in a quavering, sing-song voice, sometimes to tunes borrowed from actual hymns, folk songs or music-hall numbers, sometimes to tunes she invented on the spot. The director Jonathan Miller, who saw her perform, described the effect as a cross between Mary Poppins and Laurence Olivier's Richard III. Seamus Heaney, watching the same persona, called it a combination of Gretel and the witch — innocence and threat delivered by the same small woman in the same girlish dress.

Audiences and critics were fascinated, and being fascinated was itself a kind of reading: a decision that the strangeness on stage was performance, artistry, a persona under control. Nobody watching a woman half-sing a poem about a corpse nobody heard needed to ask what, exactly, was being signalled. The poem's own bystanders had already supplied the answer: he always loved larking.

sections.heading: The Committee That Watched Her Tear Up Her Bouquet
sections.body:
In 1967, after John Masefield died, Whitehall began sounding out candidates for Poet Laureate, and Stevie Smith's name came up. Files on the selection, declassified by the National Archives and reported in 2023, show exactly how she was read. Geoffrey Handley-Taylor, chair of the Poetry Society, dismissed her as "unstable," citing his evidence: she "sang her verses at the recent Festival Hall affair and afterwards tore her bouquet to pieces on the platform." Helen Gardner, Merton Professor of English at Oxford, went further, calling Smith "absurd" and writing that she "wrote 'little girl poetry' about herself mostly." John Betjeman got the job.

Nobody on that committee seems to have asked what tearing apart a bouquet in public might have meant, any more than the crowd at the Festival Hall had asked what a half-sung nursery rhyme about drowning might have meant, any more than Punch had asked, fourteen years earlier, why a poem calling itself touching kept insisting on saying so. Smith had described the pattern exactly in April 1953, before it happened to her twice more: not a failure to signal, but a failure, again and again, in the people close enough to have heard.
